methodological_rigor.justification: This is a single-center retrospective comparison in which groups are defined by a temporal switch (sequential before Sept 2021 vs. concomitant after), which conflates administration method with calendar-period changes in supportive care (e.g., aprepitant 77.2% vs 84.0%), referral patterns, and prior-line distribution. Baseline imbalances are large and clinically meaningful (liver metastases 70.5% vs 34.0%, metastatic recurrence 97.7% vs 74.0%, third-line or later 29.5% vs 16.0%), yet no propensity matching, IPTW, or stratified analysis is performed; the multivariate Cox is used only to adjust for a limited set of covariates with univariate p<0.1. No a priori power calculation is reported, no pre-specified primary endpoint is declared, exclusion of patients who switched between schedules may bias the Group C survival estimates upward, and no sensitivity analyses or imputation for missing CA19-9/pathology are presented. Statistically the Mann-Whitney, Fisher, log-rank, and Cox approaches are appropriate and the PH assumption was reportedly checked, but no multiplicity correction is applied to the many AE comparisons and effect sizes with CIs are inconsistently reported.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The design is an individual retrospective cohort comparing two sequentially implemented administration schedules, aligning with Oxford 2b (an individual cohort study with notable risk-of-bias features). The clinical question is practical and relevant: shortening nal-IRI + 5-FU/Levo-LV infusion from a median of 271 to 149 minutes addresses time toxicity, a patient-centered concern well-framed in the discussion. However, efficacy claims (OS 5.6 vs 8.4 months, PFS 2.1 vs 4.5 months) are confounded by non-comparable baseline prognosis, so the paper only supports the operational conclusion that concomitant administration appears feasible without an obvious safety signal. Findings may inform local protocol choices in centers already using nal-IRI/5-FU/LV but are not practice-changing and do not alter guidelines.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the applicable standard for this retrospective observational cohort. Inclusion/exclusion criteria, a patient-flow diagram (Figure 2), outcome definitions, statistical methods, missing-data acknowledgment (CA19-9 and pathology missing in two cases each), and ethics approval with opt-out consent are reported, satisfying many STROBE items. Important omissions include no explicit STROBE checklist, no description of handling of selection bias or sensitivity analyses, limited reporting of adverse-event grading per CTCAE item-by-item (relegated to Table 2), and inconsistent terminology (e.g., 'all randomized patients' in a non-randomized study). No data-availability statement, repository link, or analytic code (EZR scripts) is provided; the manuscript gives no indication that individual-level data or scripts are shareable.

novelty_literature.justification: The core comparison — concomitant vs sequential administration of nal-IRI with Levo-LV — has already been reported by Takada et al. (reference 12), and the current manuscript explicitly frames itself as confirmatory ('These findings are consistent with those of the previous study [12]'). Novelty is therefore mostly empirical and incremental: a second single-center Japanese series adding operational data on infusion time and framing results in terms of time toxicity. No new mechanism, assay, or population is introduced, and the physicochemical rationale (pH range) is derivative. The time-toxicity framing is a mild conceptual contribution but is well-trodden in the cited literature.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is organized conventionally and generally readable, with clear methods, outcome definitions, and a logical discussion that addresses confounding by prior-line and liver-metastasis imbalance. Several problems reduce clarity: the Results section states the median follow-up was for 'all randomized patients' though this is a non-randomized study; the abstract duplicates its concluding sentence verbatim; some figures/table captions (e.g., Figure 3) are terse and not fully standalone; and the abstract p-value (p<0.001) and HR CI formatting is inconsistent across sections. Overall writing is adequate but would benefit from careful editing and tighter reconciliation of narrative with the actual study design.

key_strengths: Clinically practical question with clear operational endpoint (median infusion time 271 vs 149 min, p<0.001) and relevance to time toxicity
Appropriate basic statistics (Mann-Whitney, Fisher, log-rank, Cox with PH assumption verified) and clear reporting of HRs and 95% CIs for PFS/OS
Transparent acknowledgment of key confounders (prior-line distribution, liver metastasis imbalance) in the Discussion
Patient-flow figure, defined inclusion/exclusion criteria, and dose/schedule described in sufficient detail to be replicated at a similar center
key_concerns: Group assignment by calendar period (before vs after Sept 2021) confounds administration schedule with secular changes in supportive care, referral mix, and prior-line distribution; no propensity-score or IPTW adjustment
Large and clinically meaningful baseline imbalances (liver metastases 70.5% vs 34.0%; metastatic recurrence 97.7% vs 74.0%) make the PFS/OS comparisons biased in favor of Group C
Exclusion of patients who switched schedules mid-treatment likely enriches Group C with longer-surviving responders, further biasing efficacy estimates
No power calculation, no pre-specified primary endpoint, no multiplicity correction across numerous AE comparisons, and no sensitivity analyses
Novelty is limited — the concomitant-administration safety/feasibility question has already been reported (reference 12); current work is confirmatory in a different Japanese single-center series
No data-availability or code-sharing statement; writing contains misleading language ('all randomized patients') for a non-randomized study
chief_reviewer.rationale: A competent but highly incremental single-center retrospective study with substantial residual confounding and limited novelty; appropriate for a tier-4 oncology journal after minor edits to clarify design terminology, add a data-availability statement, and strengthen caveats around confounded efficacy comparisons.
